p.title: RELINK: Edge Activation for Closed Network Influence Maximization via Deep Reinforcement Learning

ext.title: RELINK: Edge Activation for Closed Network Influence Maximization via Deep Reinforcement Learning
ext.document_type: Conference paper (full text, 8 pages of body plus references, 12-page ACM format per the reference block)
ext.coverage: Read the whole extracted text file (2,054 lines, 77,630 chars) in two chunks: lines 1-1224 and 1225-2054. Covers front matter, abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries, embedding (Sec. 4), MDP and DDQN training (Sec. 5), experiments (Sec. 6, Tables/Figures 1-6), conclusion, GenAI disclosure and the full reference list. No Paul markup was supplied for this PDF (none), so paul_markup is empty. The paper contains no lobbying, election, persuasion/turnout, legislator or text-measurement content; those topics are absent, not just unaddressed in the excerpt.
ext.research_question: How can we learn effective edge activation strategies for influence maximization in closed (privacy-constrained) social networks, where node-level activation is infeasible and propagation is limited to a budgeted subset of existing edges? (Abstract; Sec. 1)
ext.theory: No social theory is developed. The diffusion basis is the Independent Cascade (IC) model (Kempe et al. 2003, ref. [49]), with the IM-CSN formulation of Huang et al. (2022, ref. [46]) as the problem definition. Motivation is privacy-focused and invitation-only platforms (Signal, Discord, Instagram Close Friends, Slack, Nextdoor), Sec. 1. The learning side is an MDP with n-step Double DQN (van Hasselt et al. 2016, ref. [85]).
ext.data: Training: 40 synthetic graphs (10 each from Barabasi-Albert, Watts-Strogatz, stochastic block model, Erdos-Renyi), node counts 25-150 (Sec. 6.1). Testing: 20 real-world social networks, unit = network (Table 1), with sizes from Residence hall (217 nodes, 2,674 edges) to Slashdot Feb'09 (82,140 nodes, 549,202 edges). Undirected edges are converted to directed pairs (Huang et al. preprocessing). Seed sets: sampled from top 5% by degree, |S| in {5, 50, 100, 200}; budget k in {5, 10, 20}. The text reports 480 experimental configurations over the 20 networks (Sec. 6.1, 6.2). Time period of the real data is not stated. Weighting: random IC probabilities in [0,1] and uniform 0.5 (Sec. 6.1).
ext.method: Edge-level DRL for IM-CSN. (1) Influence-aware node embeddings combining five feature classes: Louvain community ID and size, approximate betweenness, degree, bridge score, clustering coefficient; path features (2-hop neighbour count, path diversity, RMPP-inspired most-probable-path feature from Chaoji et al. 2012); outgoing-edge weight mean/max/variance; seed indicators and seed distance; Node2Vec embedding; SVD reduction to d=16 (Sec. 4.1). (2) Edge-aware aggregation with learned relevance score alpha_ij = sigma(a^T[h_i||h_j] * w_ij), two-hop aggregation via A^2, gated update and degree-normalized residual (Sec. 4.2). (3) MDP: state = partial subgraph, action = activate an edge respecting the per-node out-degree budget k, reward = exact marginal influence gain under IC (Sec. 5.1). (4) Edge Q-values from projected node features, edge weight, and a penalty on accumulated incoming weight (Sec. 5.2). (5) Training by n-step Double DQN with EMA target network, replay buffer of 1M transitions, epsilon-greedy exploration, valid-action restriction; true marginal gains are computed only at training time (Sec. 5.3). (6) Inference: greedy argmax over action-masked Q-values, one edge per step, until no valid actions remain; max steps O(|V|k) (Sec. 5.4). Hardware: NVIDIA A40 GPU, Xeon Silver 4314 CPU; PyTorch, Adam (Sec. 6.1). Baselines: Degree, FoF, Random (five-run average), PSNA (Huang et al. 2022) (Sec. 6.1).
ext.identification: None in the causal sense. This is a simulation benchmark. A single RELINK model is trained once on synthetic graphs and evaluated on 20 unseen real networks across all seed-set and budget settings (Sec. 6.1, 6.2). Out-of-distribution generalization is the claimed identification logic, not a designed comparison of causal effects.
ext.scope: Population: online and privacy-constrained social networks (messaging, trust, email, Facebook/ego, music and voting-style networks, per Table 1). Diffusion: IC only in all experiments (Sec. 6.1). Era: not stated. Institutional setting: academic benchmark on public network datasets; no platform or firm data. Other diffusion models (LT, Trigger, WC) are described as adaptable by changing the reward, but not tested (footnote 1, Sec. 6.1).

key_findings.finding: RELINK achieves higher average influence spread than Random, Degree, and FoF in most configurations.
key_findings.numbers: Wins out of 480: vs Random 462, vs Degree 464, vs FoF 462. Text says it consistently outperforms all methods in at least 90% of experiments.

key_findings.finding: RELINK outperforms the IM-CSN-specific baseline PSNA in most experiments.
key_findings.numbers: RELINK better in 456 of 480; PSNA better in 24 of 480.

key_findings.finding: RELINK's advantage is largest under small edge budgets; the gap to PSNA narrows as k grows.
key_findings.numbers: Heatmap colour scale 0.85 to 1.15 (ratio). Text says improvements frequently exceed 15%. Dense graphs (email-Eu-core, wiki-Vote, sx-mathoverflow) favour PSNA at smaller seed sets.

key_findings.finding: Under k=20 and uniform weights, RELINK attains the highest spread when seed sets are small; baseline ordering is Random and PSNA best, then FoF and Degree.
key_findings.location: Sec. 6.2 (Figure 4 panels a-j, k=20, uniform weights)
key_findings.numbers: Figure-only values; no numeric table of means in the text.

key_findings.finding: Runtime: RELINK is slower on small and medium graphs but becomes competitive with or faster than PSNA as graph size grows; the Random, Degree and FoF baselines are cheapest.
key_findings.numbers: Figure-only; text gives PSNA complexity O(I(|V|+|E|) log|V| + |V| d_m log d_m).

key_findings.finding: Training is expensive because exact marginal gains are computed during training; inference needs no spread estimation.
key_findings.numbers: 6,257.329 seconds for 2,000 epochs, a single model reused across all experiments.

key_findings.finding: Headline gain claim in the abstract: up to 15% higher spread, with improved scalability.
key_findings.location: Abstract; Sec. 6.3 says 'frequently achieving influence spread improvements exceeding 15%'
key_findings.numbers: Abstract: 'up to 15%'. Body: 'exceeding 15%' in frequent cases. The two statements are not identical.

limitations: Stated by authors (Sec. 7): extension to dynamic or time-evolving topologies, adaptive constraints, user-specific constraints, and uncertainty in diffusion models are left to future work.
Stated by authors (Sec. 7): sample-efficient training and theoretical analysis of policy optimality under submodular objectives are not addressed; no optimality guarantee is claimed.
Stated by authors (Sec. 6.1): all experiments use the IC model only; LT, Trigger and WC are described as adaptable but untested (footnote 1).
Stated by authors (Sec. 6.4): training takes 6,257.329 s because exact marginal gains are computed during training.
Stated by authors (Sec. 6.2, Q3): RELINK has higher runtime on small and medium graphs, with a fixed embedding overhead.
Stated by authors (Sec. 5.1): the objective is non-submodular and the greedy/IC marginal-gain computation is costly; the method computes exact gains only at training time.
Reviewer note (not stated by authors): the abstract says 'up to 15% higher influence spread' while Sec. 6.3 says improvements 'frequently' exceed 15%; these are different claims.

Reviewer note (not stated by authors): 480 configurations do not follow from the stated grid (20 networks x 3 k values x 4 seed sizes = 240). The text does not explain the factor of two, which may come from the two weighting schemes, but it does not say so.

Reviewer note (not stated by authors): results are reported as win counts and figure curves, with no numeric tables, confidence intervals or variance across the 10 repeats, so effect sizes are only partly recoverable from the text.

Reviewer note (not stated by authors): the training graphs are synthetic and the test graphs are public real networks; no closed-network or platform-private data are used, so 'closed network' is simulated by constraining propagation to chosen edges.
measures: Average influence spread under IC, estimated with 100,000 Monte Carlo simulations, repeated 10 times (Sec. 6.1)
Win counts out of 480 experiments for pairwise method comparison (Figure 3)
Marginal influence gain as the per-step reward (Definition 1, Sec. 5.1)
Edge budget k in {5,10,20}; seed-set size |S| in {5,50,100,200}
Node embedding dimension d=16 via SVD

short_quotes.quote: the first DRL framework for edge-level influence maximization in privacy-constrained networks

rel.summary_md:
RELINK (Arya, Ghosh, Maruyama and Srinivasan, CIKM 2025) treats influence maximization in "closed" networks as an edge-selection problem. The seed set is fixed, and each node may switch on at most k of its outgoing edges. Spread can travel only along the edges that were switched on. The method builds influence-aware node embeddings and trains an edge-scoring Double DQN on 40 small synthetic graphs (25-150 nodes). The same trained policy then runs on 20 public real networks. Spread is simulated under Independent Cascade (IC) with random or uniform 0.5 edge weights, using 100,000 Monte Carlo draws repeated 10 times. RELINK beats Random, Degree and FoF in about 462-464 of 480 configurations, and beats the IM-CSN baseline PSNA in 456 of 480. The margin is widest at small edge budgets and narrows as k grows. On dense graphs PSNA can win at small seed sets. RELINK is slower than PSNA on small and medium graphs and only catches up on large ones. The paper offers no optimality guarantee and says the objective is non-submodular. No legislative, lobbying or empirical-persuasion data are involved.

The paper matters here because Melange already names RELINK as the design source for its cosponsor recruitment routes. These are `cosponsor_route.py` (champion seeds, at most K=5 asks per recruiter) and the dashboard's closed-network Max-cascade route (`closedCascadeRoute`, 6 edges, fan-out 2). What the system took is the problem framing: an action is an edge, and each node has an out-degree budget. It did not take the learned policy or any of RELINK's evidence. Both builds are hand-tuned greedy heuristics. They are close relatives of the baselines RELINK outperforms, applied to a dense 533-node graph that sits in the regime where RELINK's edge is smallest. The paper therefore supports the code's own disclaimer that no (1-1/e) guarantee applies. It gives no empirical support for K, the fan-out or the kernel probabilities. It also weakens the case for replacing the money optimizer with a learned policy, because that optimizer's greedy is already exact for its separable concave objective. Everything in this mapping is agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: IM-CSN as edge activation: seeds are fixed, each node may activate at most k of its out-edges (k in {5,10,20}), and the reward is the marginal IC spread. A DRL edge policy beats Random, Degree and FoF in 462-464 of 480 configurations and PSNA in 456 of 480. Gains reach about 15%, mainly at small k.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3 and 5.1 (MDP, per-node out-degree budget); Sec. 6.2-6.3, Figures 3 and 6
bearings.system_side: The docstring credits 'RELINK + MOPBD*'. Champion seeds each whip at most K=5 colleagues (out-degree budget). The recruiter list is built greedily, ranked by a value-per-dollar score (gain - lambda(1-p))/cost for lambda in {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}, and a Pareto front is taken. The optional MC reach runs IC over the induced node subgraph of seeds plus recruits. That is all edges among those nodes, not only the activated edges as IM-CSN requires. K=5 and CEDGE are unestimated dials.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the problem formulation transfers: edge actions under a per-node budget. The performance evidence does not. RELINK's wins are for a trained DDQN policy, and this component is a greedy heuristic. The spread being maximized is simulated IC on public online graphs with random or uniform 0.5 weights. Melange's kernel probabilities (x/(x+6), with an unestimated saturation constant) are mostly lower, a regime the paper never tested. The paper also has no evidence that a per-legislator 'whip capacity' K exists or is near 5. Treat the whip capacity as a modeling prior.

bearings.paper_claim: The IM-CSN objective is non-submodular, so greedy marginal-gain edge selection carries no approximation guarantee. Among heuristics, Degree ranks last with FoF next to it under k=20 uniform weights, and Random and PSNA do best. On dense graphs (email-Eu-core, wiki-Vote, sx-mathoverflow) RELINK's advantage over PSNA reverses at small seed sets.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.1 (non-submodular objective); Sec. 6.2 Figure 4 (k=20 baseline ordering); Sec. 6.3 Figure 6 (dense-graph cases)
bearings.system_side: The dashboard Max-cascade route grows a closed-network edge tree from the selected member: 6 edges, at most 2 asks per recruiter. Each edge is scored as arrival x marginal x (0.75 + 0.25 PR/PRMAX), and the code says it makes no (1-1/e) claim. budgetRecruit is a node-seed max-coverage greedy that does claim (1-1/e) on its submodular coverage proxy. A test pins the hub-convergence disclosure ruling.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Two parts carry over: the non-submodularity point, and the warning that degree- or hub-favouring heuristics are weak under per-node edge budgets. Both are structural and support the code's existing disclaimer. The (1-1/e) claim on budgetRecruit holds only for its node-coverage proxy, not for an edge-activation spread. The paper does not show whether hub convergence in a 533-node House cosponsor graph is good or bad, because dense small graphs are where its comparisons were least favourable to RELINK. Treat the route outputs as heuristic model outputs, never as introduction or access probabilities.

bearings.paper_claim: The learned edge policy is slower than PSNA on small and medium graphs. It becomes competitive or faster only as graphs grow to tens of thousands of nodes. Training cost 6,257 s because exact marginal gains are computed. The gains come in a non-submodular combinatorial setting.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 6.2 Q3 (Figure 5, runtime); Sec. 6.4 (training cost); Sec. 5.1
bearings.system_side: CELF lazy greedy over per-member concave dollar chunks. The docstring states that in a fixed stance state the objective is separable and concave, so greedy is the exact discrete optimum. A Golovin-Krause bound is kept as a diagnostic. The dashboard's budgetRecruit comment already says 'no ML needed at our scale'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: RELINK's case for a learned policy rests on scale and on non-submodular edge choice. Neither applies to a 533-member, separable, concave money allocation, where greedy is already exact. A learned policy could matter only for the conversion-replanning path, which is not certified, or for a future edge-level recruitment optimizer. Even then the paper's evidence comes from synthetic IC benchmarks, not legislative outcomes.

bearings.paper_claim: Spread is estimated with 100,000 Monte Carlo IC simulations, repeated 10 times, to separate methods whose spread ratios fall roughly between 0.85 and 1.15.
bearings.system_side: Competitive IC uses keyed splitmix64 common random numbers, with MC=20 for the frontier and MC=40 for the scenario and route runs. The splitmix64 draw function is sm64, and the shared kernel is build_P.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a benchmark for how many simulations are needed to resolve differences of 5-15% between alternatives. CRN reduces variance in paired comparisons, so far fewer draws may be enough for rank decisions. Comparing absolute spreads across routes or Pareto points at MC 20-40 is not supported by this paper. The adequacy of MC=20-40 is still the system's own claim (mc_stability_check), and this paper does not test it.

gaps_exposed: No learned or optimized edge-activation policy exists. Both RELINK-labelled builds (cosponsor_route.py and closedCascadeRoute) are greedy heuristics like the baselines RELINK beats. Neither has been compared against even a Random edge baseline, which ranked among the strongest heuristics in RELINK's Figure 4.

cosponsor_route.py mc_spread lets activation run over every edge among the selected nodes, not only the activated edges. That is not the IM-CSN closed-network semantics the docstring claims. The dashboard Max route's cascadeReach then runs an open-network cascade from the recruited set.

The per-recruiter budgets (K=5 in cosponsor_route, fanout=2 and edgeBudget=6 in the dashboard) are not estimated from any observed whip or ask behaviour, and the paper gives no basis for legislative values.
There is no sensitivity check of route rankings to the budget k. RELINK shows method ordering changes with k (its gap to PSNA narrows as k grows).
The paper's evidence is IC-only, with random or uniform 0.5 weights. The system's low-probability kernel regime (crypto p_max 0.23, CU 0.52) is untested territory for any edge-activation claim.
flags: Labelling caution: the code and brain call these routes the 'RELINK design' and 'RELINK Pareto' (cosponsor_route.py:3; make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:675,828; brain topic 2026-06-feature-melange-scenario-model-build). The system borrows only the problem framing. No RELINK performance result transfers to these heuristics, so any claim citing RELINK's '15%' or '456/480' for Melange routes would be a misattribution.

Route outputs (expected recruits, 'all asks hold' percentages, Pareto spread) are heuristic model outputs under unestimated ASKM, K and kernel constants. Under D-025 they must not be presented as introduction, access or closeness probabilities.

The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization), so there is nothing to flag there. It uses no LDA data, so D-021 does not apply.
This whole mapping is agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces it.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. His nearest positions concern the joint optimizer, the budget frontier and the cosponsor route. For the optimizer he expects a learned policy (GCOMB) to replace greedy at scale. RELINK is a learned edge policy, but it pays off on runtime only for graphs much larger than the 533-member House. Its spread advantage comes in a non-submodular setting. The joint optimizer's separable concave money problem is neither, so greedy is already exact there. On that component Paul's expectation runs ahead of what this evidence supports, and the system's own 'no ML needed at our scale' comment matches the paper better. On the cosponsor route, Paul said D* Lite and LPA* replanning should be the operational layer. RELINK is silent on incremental replanning, so that gap remains. RELINK did supply the per-recruiter budget idea that was built. The brain records RELINK in the June 2026 research corpus as 'maps to co-sponsor campaigns'. That note is not wrong but is incomplete: it does not say that the built version is a greedy heuristic rather than RELINK's DRL, or that RELINK's evidence covers synthetic IC spread on public online graphs, not legislators.

related.why: cosponsor_route.py cites RELINK and MOPBD* together. RELINK supplies the edge-budget formulation and MOPBD* the multi-objective Pareto routing concept.
Same family of reinforcement learning for influence maximization. Chen's contingency-aware seeding is implemented as the seed gate, while RELINK's edge policy is borrowed only as a formulation.
Another DRL influence-maximization policy, for complex contagion, the alternative to RELINK's IC-only setting that Paul raises for coalition formation.
Learned influence-maximization policies under limited network access. It is the node-and-sampling analogue of RELINK's constraint of propagating only along chosen edges.
Graph-embedding and GNN influence maximization. RELINK's node2vec, SVD and edge-aware aggregation embedding sits in the same lineage.
Golovin-Krause guarantees need (adaptive) submodularity. RELINK states that IM-CSN is non-submodular and claims no guarantee, so those bounds do not extend to edge-activation routes.

Likely the 2026 Scientific Reports benchmark the dashboard cites for using a PageRank prior in route scoring. Its heuristic-versus-greedy findings sit beside RELINK's learned-versus-heuristic results.
Both build on Kempe-style IC cascades. Bharathi's competitive IC is the system's coalition cascade, while RELINK's edge activation assumes a single cascade.
Both evaluate influence maximization under the Independent Cascade model, using Monte Carlo spread estimates as the outcome.
